opus-5.5.text:
I think the core reason is that long context isn't really a capability you get just by making the window bigger. In pre-training, you can extend the context length, and the model will technically be able to attend to a hundred thousand or a million tokens. But being able to *see* that many tokens and being able to *use* them well are two very different things.

What we actually care about is whether the model can do long-horizon tasks: reading a large codebase and making a coherent change, working through a long research problem, or acting as an agent over many steps where what it did fifty steps ago still matters. Those tasks need the model to know what to remember, what to ignore, when to go back and check something, and how to keep a plan consistent over time. That's much more about behavior and strategy than about raw memory capacity.

Pre-training data mostly doesn't contain that kind of signal. Most documents on the internet are short, and even the long ones aren't structured as "here's a long task, and here's how you successfully complete it while managing all this information." So the model learns local patterns very well, but it doesn't naturally learn how to operate over long horizons.

Post-training, especially reinforcement learning, lets you directly optimize for the outcome. You put the model in an environment where the task actually requires using a lot of context, and you reward it when it succeeds. Then the model can discover its own ways of handling that context, like summarizing, taking notes, revisiting earlier information, or breaking the problem into parts. Those are skills you'd struggle to hand-design or to get from imitation alone.

There's also an efficiency argument. Scaling pre-training context is very expensive, and you pay that cost for every token whether it's useful or not. In post-training, you can focus compute on exactly the behaviors that matter. And I think in the long run, the more interesting question isn't "how long is your context window" but "how well can your model work on a task that takes hours or days." That's fundamentally a post-training and RL question.

So I'm not saying pre-training doesn't matter. You need a good base with reasonable context support. But the part that turns long context into real capability, I believe, mostly comes from post-training.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is: long-context ability is less about architecture and more about behavior. The pretraining stage gives you a model that has absorbed an enormous amount of knowledge and can process a long window of tokens, but that doesn't mean it knows what to do with a long task. Reading a long document and actually working through a long problem are different things. Long-horizon tasks require the model to decide what to pay attention to, what to remember, what to write down, when to stop and reconsider, and when to go look something up again. Those are skills, not just capacities.

If you try to solve this purely at the pretraining or architecture level, you end up fighting a very expensive battle. You can extend the window, change the attention mechanism, add memory modules, but the data in pretraining is just text that happens to be long. It doesn't contain many examples of an agent managing its own context over thousands of steps, because humans don't write that down. So the model never really sees the process of a long task being executed. It sees the outputs.

Post-training is where you can actually teach that process. With reinforcement learning or well-designed interactive data, you put the model in an environment where it has to act over many turns, where the reward depends on getting the whole thing right, not just the next token. Then the model learns things like summarizing its own state, taking notes, using tools to offload memory, or breaking a task into stages. In my experience from the ReAct and tree-of-thought work, a lot of what looked like a capability limit was really a lack of training signal on the right behavior. Once the model is trained to reason and act in loops, the effective horizon it can handle grows much faster than the raw context window does.

There's also a very practical argument. Post-training is cheaper and faster to iterate on. You can run experiments in days rather than months, and you can target specific failure modes you observe in real agents. And the gains compound with whatever base model you have. If a better architecture comes along, the post-training recipe still applies on top of it.

So my view is that the context window is a resource, and post-training is how you teach the model to manage that resource well. The bottleneck for long tasks right now is not that models can't hold enough tokens. It's that they haven't been trained enough on what to do with them.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between having a long context window and actually being able to use it. You can train a model to accept more tokens, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it can find the relevant information, connect evidence across the context, or carry out a task reliably.

That’s why I’m interested in post-training. It lets us optimize for what we actually want the model to do. If a task requires reading a lot of material and producing a correct answer, we can train on that outcome, rather than assuming that better next-token prediction over long sequences will automatically produce the right behavior.

There’s also a broader point: some long-context problems can be approached through interaction. A model can search, retrieve, take notes, and revisit information instead of processing everything in one pass. Post-training gives us a way to teach those strategies. So I see it as complementary to extending the context window: the window provides capacity, and post-training helps turn that capacity into useful behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between being able to fit a long context and being able to use it effectively. A larger context window gives the model access to more information, but it doesn’t automatically teach the model what to look for, which details to retain, or how to connect evidence across a long input.

That’s why I’m interested in post-training. You can train on tasks where success actually depends on using information from different parts of the context, and reward the model for getting the task right. That gives you a more direct signal about the behavior you want than simply training on longer sequences.

There’s also an interaction with agents. For a long-running task, you don’t necessarily want to put every observation into the context forever. The model needs to learn when to retrieve information, when to summarize, and when to revisit something it saw earlier. Those are decisions, and post-training is a natural way to improve them. So I see longer context as an important capability, and post-training as a way to turn that capability into useful behavior.
